title: Seal of Liberties
setting: Westminster, England, October 1297, during Edward I's confirmation of Magna Carta by letters patent.
description: You are a clerk in the royal chancery as Edward I renews the Great Charter. The text before you confirms liberties for the Church, barons and freemen, yet it also records a tax grant to the king. Hear each interest, inspect key clauses, and decide how the confirmation should be framed: as a bargain for cooperation, a curb on royal power, or a narrow defence of rank and custom.
learningObjectives: Explain what Magna Carta promised about justice, taxation and the rights of free men.
Describe why barons, church and king each wanted the charter confirmed or resisted.
Evaluate whose interests the charter protected.

player.name: Unnamed Chancery Clerk
player.brief: You hear petitions, compare clauses, and draft the notes that shape how the confirmation is understood.

sharedContext.text: Edward's letters say he has inspected the Great Charter and now confirms it again. The same record says the realm granted the king a fifteenth of movable goods for these liberties. Your task is to hear how crown, church, magnates and freemen read the charter, then decide what meaning your draft will carry into the final confirmation.

decision.title: How should the opening memorandum frame the confirmation?
decision.prompt: Your first draft will guide everyone who reads the charter in this hearing. If you tie liberties to the tax grant, you may keep the process moving. If you stress hard legal limits first, you may sharpen the charter's force but test royal patience.

options.label: Draft the opening around mutual grant and service.
Draft the opening around clause 29 and the danger of delay.
Draft the opening as a restatement of ancient custom.

sharedContext.text: Now the issue is detail. Some clauses fix where pleas should be heard. Others limit amercements, officials and legal sale. The charter also preserves scutage as it was in the time of Henry II. Your digest must show whether confirmation means tighter justice or a safer version of old practice.

decision.title: What final note will go forward with the sealed confirmation?
decision.prompt: The letters patent are ready, but your cover note will guide how others understand them. Will you present the confirmation as a broad settlement for the realm, or centre it on ranked liberties and customary restraint?

endings.title: Dismissed Before the Seal
endings.summary: Your memorandum puts clause 29 ahead of the political bargain. The language is admired by some readers, but the crown removes you from the drafting process before the final text is settled.

historicalOutcome.text: The surviving record does not show the confirmation collapsing at this point. Instead, Edward says he 'conceed and confirm' the grants and wishes the charter to be 'firmly and inviably observed' in perpetuity.

spans.quote: conceed and confirm them for ourselves and our heirs
the aforesaid charter is to be firmly and inviably observed in all and each of its articles in perpetuity

endings.divergence: This ending diverges from the record. Your removal from the process is a simulation assumption used to show how fragile access to power could be.
reflectionQuestions: Why might a crown accept the charter in writing but resist a hard public reading of it?
Which is more effective in politics: a strong principle, or a principle phrased in acceptable language?
Who loses most if a clerk is shut out before the final wording is fixed?

endings.title: Talks Stall in the Drafting Room
endings.summary: You circulate the clauses in their hardest possible form. Instead of moving toward the seal, the room freezes. No one trusts the next step, and your influence ends in a procedural deadlock.

historicalOutcome.text: The charter text itself records a different outcome. It says the realm 'have given us a fifteenth part of all their movable goods,' and Edward then 'conceed and confirm' the grants in letters patent.

endings.divergence: This ending diverges from the record. The real text reaches confirmation; the stalled talks are a counterfactual branch.
reflectionQuestions: Why might some supporters of liberty still prefer a softer draft?

Does a stricter reading always produce a stronger result?

endings.title: Confirmed in Perpetuity
endings.summary: Your final note presents the charter as a broad settlement: liberties for church, magnates and freemen, tied to a political bargain the king can accept. The seal goes on, and your reading stays close to the surviving record.

historicalOutcome.text: The record states that the realm 'have given us a fifteenth part of all their movable goods.' Edward then declares that he 'conceed and confirm' the grants and wants the charter 'firmly and inviably observed in all and each of its articles in perpetuity.'
